title: Strong matchgate designs in nearly optimal depth
authors: Maxwell West, M. Cerezo, Martin Larocca
abstract: Understanding the resources required to generate approximately random unitaries over various groups is a natural goal of quantum information theory. With respect to one notion of approximation, that of a design, it is known that the full unitary group can be approximated in logarithmic depth by one-dimensional circuits of nearest-neighbour 2-local gates. On the other hand, remarkably, circuits with this connectivity cannot form designs over the matchgate group in sublinear depth. Here we show that this dramatic slowdown can disappear when using a general qubit connectivity graph $\mathsf{G}$ of routing number ${\rm rt}(\mathsf{G})$. Indeed, in this setting one can obtain (strong) $\varepsilon$-approximate relative error matchgate $k$-designs in depth $\mathcal{O}(k^2{\rm rt}(\mathsf{G})\log n\log(n/\varepsilon))$. For all-to-all connectivity, ${\rm rt}(\mathsf{G})=2$. Our construction is conceptually simple, involving a random walk on the matchgate group, and no ancillae. As a technical byproduct, we improve upon the state of the art for fermionic routing, obtaining an $\mathcal{O}({\rm rt}(\mathsf{G})\log n)$ depth router. Additionally, for $k=3$, we obtain an exact strong matchgate design in $\mathcal{O}({\rm rt}(\mathsf{G})\log n)$ depth, again without ancillae. Under all-to-all connectivity, our fermionic router and 3-designs are optimal. Notably, our results imply that quantum algorithms for fermionic tomography which require drawing from a matchgate 3-design may be exponentially sped up on quantum computers with all-to-all connectivity, relative to their strictly one-dimensional counterparts.
summary: This paper develops methods to construct high-quality quantum states (k-designs) over the matchgate group, which is relevant for quantum simulation and tomography. It achieves this by analyzing the depth required based on the underlying quantum hardware's connectivity graph. The key finding is that the required depth scales polynomially with $k$ and the graph's routing number, offering significant speedups over previous theoretical limits.
main_problem: The paper addresses the resource cost (circuit depth) required to generate approximately random unitaries, specifically $k$-designs, over the matchgate group on quantum hardware.
main_result: They provide a construction achieving strong $\epsilon$-approximate relative error matchgate $k$-designs in depth $O(k^2 r_t(G) \log n \log(n/\epsilon))$ for general connectivity, and show optimal depth for $k=3$ in the all-to-all case.
method: The construction uses a random walk on the matchgate group, followed by compiling the resulting operations into quantum circuits using techniques related to fermionic routing and Clifford group gates.
model_or_system: The system involves $n$ qubits and the matchgate group $MG(n)$, which is generated by 2-Majorana rotations. The complexity is analyzed based on the connectivity graph $G$ and its routing number $r_t(G)$.
key_observables: Design quality ($\epsilon$-approximate relative error $k$-design), circuit depth ($D$), and the routing number $r_t(G)$.
important_parameters: Number of qubits ($n$), design order ($k$), approximation error ($\epsilon$), and graph connectivity ($r_t(G)$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on spectral bounds derived from the random walk operator and the ability to compile permutations using Clifford gates, with the general case overcoming limitations of nearest-neighbor connectivity.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the three-step construction process: sampling rotations, checking for parallelization into layers, and compiling layers into two-qubit gates. Figure (A) shows the structure of a binary tree for $n=3$ qubits.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general depth bound for $k$-designs using random walks. It then details the compilation of permutations of Majoranas into depth $O(r_t(G) \log n)$ using Clifford gates. Finally, it provides lower bounds on the required depth for $k$-designs.
why_interesting: The results provide concrete, resource-aware estimates for implementing complex quantum tasks (like tomography) on near-term hardware architectures by optimizing the required circuit depth based on physical connectivity.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Our construction proceeds in three steps: (1) Randomly sample m ∈O(k2n log(n/ε)) pairs 1 ⩽ai < bi ⩽2n, and m angles ϑi; apply the corresponding Majorana rotations {Rai,bi(ϑi)}m i=1. (2) Check if those rotations can be parallelised into O(k2 log(n/ε)) layers of commuting gates; if not, go back to step one. (3) Compile each parallel layer of Majorana rotations into two qubit gates of depth O(rt(G) log n) via a fermionic router. Concatenate two such independently accepted circuits; the total depth is then given by (# Layers) × O(rt(G) log n) = O(k2rt(G) log(n/ε) log n).
